paragraphs.text: Early-onset dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia is an autosomal dominant neurologic disorder. Affected individuals have spasticity or pyramidal signs, dystonia, or both. Dystonia ranges from isolated upper-limb involvement to generalized dystonia. A few patients also have developmental delay or intellectual disability (Gilbert et al., 2009; Zech et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Gilbert et al. (2009) reported a large multigenerational kindred from Ohio with a highly penetrant autosomal dominant neurologic disorder that caused spasticity and dystonia. Onset of spasticity and weakness ranged from the first year of life to the sixth decade. Onset of dystonia ranged from the first to the third decade. Affected individuals had no ataxia and no apparent cognitive involvement. Neuroimaging and peripheral neurophysiology were normal.

paragraphs.text: Zech et al. (2022) described 3 unrelated patients (patients 8 to 10) with de novo heterozygous ATP5MC3 mutations. Patient 8 was a previously reported 12-year-old boy with isolated upper-limb dystonia. Patient 9 was a 15-year-old girl with a history of delayed milestones, pyramidal signs, and generalized dystonia that mainly affected the upper body. Patient 10 was a 6-year-old boy with delayed psychomotor development, lower-limb spasticity, and raised blood lactate. Zech et al. (2022) combined these 3 patients with a previously reported multigenerational family in which 15 members had clinical information. Of these 18 individuals, 12 had dystonia, 17 had spasticity or pyramidal signs, and 2 had developmental delay or intellectual disability. Ten individuals had a dystonia-predominant syndrome. The authors noted that patients 9 and 10 confirmed spastic symptoms in independent families. These 2 patients were also the first to show neurodevelopmental comorbidity, which pointed to relevant phenotypic differences between unrelated families.

paragraphs.text: Gilbert et al. (2009) performed single-point and multipoint linkage analysis in the Ohio kindred, using microsatellite and SNP array genotyping. They mapped the disease locus to chromosome 2q24-q31, between flanking markers rs1424937 and rs1559510. The region lies proximal to SPG13 and contains no known hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) or dystonia genes. In a secondary analysis, they searched for candidate genes that segregated with the dystonia phenotype and found 2 candidate regions with parametric lod scores above 2.0.

paragraphs.text: Zech et al. (2022) used exome sequencing of mitochondrial disease and dystonia cohorts to identify de novo heterozygous missense mutations in the ATP5MC3 gene in 3 unrelated patients. Patient 8, a 12-year-old boy with isolated upper-limb dystonia, carried an N106K mutation. The authors noted that this mutation had also been found in an unrelated multigenerational family in which 18 of 40 relatives had dystonia and/or spasticity. Patient 9, a girl with delayed milestones, pyramidal signs, and generalized dystonia, carried a P107A mutation. Patient 10, a boy with delayed psychomotor development, lower-limb spasticity, and raised blood lactate, carried a G79V mutation. None of the 3 mutations was present in gnomAD. Structural modeling placed Asn106 and Pro107 at the interaction site between the FO and F1 subcomplexes, and predicted that G79V would disrupt a contact between helices in the c-ring. In fibroblasts from patient 8, ATPase activity was slightly but significantly decreased and the oxygen consumption rate was reduced. In fibroblasts from patient 10, ATPase enzyme activity was deficient, and BN-PAGE showed a moderate decrease in assembled ATPase. All 3 substitutions affected strictly conserved residues that lie close together in the C-terminal helical motifs of the protein, and 2 of them were at directly neighboring nucleotides. Zech et al. (2022) concluded that these findings broadened the range of disease-associated ATP5MC3 genotypes and strengthened the link between the gene and disease.

Structural modeling placed Asn106 at the interaction site between the FO and F1 subcomplexes. In the patient's fibroblasts, ATPase activity was slightly but significantly decreased and the oxygen consumption rate was reduced. The ATPase enzyme deficit was significantly smaller than that caused by the G79V mutation.

checks.claim: The ATPase deficit caused by the ATP5MC3 G79V mutation was significantly larger than that caused by the N106K mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: produced a significantly greater ATPase enzyme deficit than ATP5MC3 c.318C>G
